curves.label: Carnot cycle
curves.ask: What are the four processes of the Carnot cycle?

explain.say: In 1824 a young French engineer, Sadi Carnot, asked a big question: what is the best a steam engine could ever do? His answer applies to every heat engine today, from car engines to power stations. He imagined a perfect cycle with no friction and no wasted temperature gaps. Look at its four sides.

curves.label: Carnot cycle
curves.ask: What are the four processes of the Carnot cycle?

draw.text: Ideal gas between 600 K and 300 K

explain.say: Side one, from 1 to 2: the gas expands at the hot temperature, 600 kelvin, taking in heat. Side two: it keeps expanding with no heat, cooling adiabatically to 300 kelvin. See the long drop on the right? Side three: it is compressed at 300 kelvin, giving heat to the cold sink. How does it get back to the start?

curves.label: Carnot cycle
curves.ask: What are the four processes of the Carnot cycle?

draw.text: 1→2 hot isothermal, 2→3 adiabatic, 3→4 cold isothermal, 4→1 adiabatic

explain.say: Side four: an adiabatic compression heats it back to 600 kelvin. The enclosed area is the net work. Carnot proved the efficiency depends only on the two temperatures, in kelvin: 1 minus T cold over T hot. Here that is 1 minus 300 over 600: exactly 50 percent. See half the heat becoming work?

outputs.label: Heat to 300 K sink
outputs.ask: Why must some heat go to the cold sink?

explain.say: The other half must go to the cold sink, as the second law demands. In our cycle, 69.3 kilojoules come in at the hot side, so 34.7 kilojoules come out as work. No real engine between these temperatures can beat this, because any friction or leak creates entropy. How could you raise the efficiency?

outputs.label: Heat to 300 K sink
outputs.ask: Why must some heat go to the cold sink?

explain.say: Make the hot side hotter or the cold side colder! A coal plant with steam at 840 kelvin and a river at 300 kelvin has a Carnot limit of 64 percent; real ones manage about 40. Superb! Exam tip: always use kelvin in the Carnot formula, never Celsius. Challenge: what is the limit between 500 and 20 degrees Celsius?

faq.q: What are the four processes of the Carnot cycle?
faq.a: Reversible isothermal expansion at the hot temperature, reversible adiabatic expansion, reversible isothermal compression at the cold temperature, and reversible adiabatic compression back to the start.
asks: what does the Carnot cycle look like

faq.q: What is the Carnot efficiency formula?
faq.a: Efficiency equals 1 minus T cold over T hot, with both temperatures in kelvin. It depends only on the source and sink temperatures.

faq.q: Why can no engine beat the Carnot efficiency?
faq.a: A more efficient engine could be paired with a reversed Carnot engine to turn heat fully into work, breaking the second law. Real engines also lose work to friction and other irreversibilities.

faq.q: Why must some heat go to the cold sink?
faq.a: Taking heat from the hot source lowers its entropy. Rejecting heat to the cold sink raises entropy enough that the total does not fall.

faq.q: Why must temperatures be in kelvin?
faq.a: The Carnot formula uses absolute temperature, a ratio from absolute zero. Celsius values give wrong answers, and even negative ones.

facts: Sadi Carnot published his analysis of heat engines in 1824.
No heat engine operating between two reservoirs can be more efficient than a reversible engine between the same reservoirs.

quiz.say: An engine works between 800 kelvin and 300 kelvin. What is its Carnot efficiency?
quiz.show: Engine between 800 K and 300 K. Carnot efficiency?

wrong.1: That is T cold over T hot, the fraction rejected, not the efficiency.
wrong.2: The second law forbids 100 percent unless the sink is at absolute zero.

quiz.say: An inventor claims an engine between 400 and 300 kelvin is 40 percent efficient. Is that possible?
quiz.show: An engine between 400 K and 300 K is claimed to be 40% efficient. Possible?

options.show: Yes, if it uses a better fuel
options.say: Yes, if it uses a better fuel

quiz.why: Carnot limit = 1 − 300/400 = 25%, so 40 percent breaks the second law.

wrong.1: Being below 100 percent is not enough; the Carnot limit is lower.
wrong.2: The limit depends only on the temperatures, not on the fuel.
